extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and critics interested in narrative method and point-of-view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative method (pictorial vs dramatic), point of view, and the dramatization or containment of the narrator within novels. Emphasizes when to use first-person, how to authenticate the narrator, and how to balance scene and summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial versus dramatic method
rubrics_metrics.description: So much of a novel, therefore, as is not dramatic enactment, not scenic, inclines always to picture, to the reflection of somebody's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the two broad modes: pictorial/chronicle (broad vistas, memory, reflection) and dramatic/scenic (enacted episodes). Most novelists use both; quality depends on management of transitions between the two. Examples: Thackeray and Fielding/Balzac/George Eliot as pictorial; Tolstoy and Dostoevsky as scenic. Use pictorial method to cover wide spans of experience; use dramatic method for intensity and climactic emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a conspicuous omniscient author
rubrics_metrics.description: The pictorial method... drags in the omniscient author and may make him exceedingly conspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conspicuous, unaccountable authorial voice can give the book an 'inconclusive look' and draw attention away from the story. Prevent thinness and loss of authority by either disguising the authorial presence or integrating the point of view into the work itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the point of view accountable (include narrator in the book)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the point of view is definitely included in the book, when it can be recognized and verified there, then every side of the book is equally wrought and fashioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticate the knowing mind and seeing eye by making them verifiable elements of the fiction (e.g., a named narrator, first-person register, or dramatized act of remembering) so readers cannot legitimately question whose knowledge the narration rests on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the 'seeing eye' (dramatize the narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to silence the question is somehow to make the mind and the eye objective, to make them facts in the story... it would then be like a play within a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn recollection, memory, or the act of narration into an onstage activity — let the narrator's recall be enacted or positioned as an event — so that the narrator's authority is part of the fiction’s fabric. Methods include first-person narration in-character and framing devices that present the narrator as a perceptible actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person ('characterized I') for precision and individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The characterized 'I' is substituted for the loose and general 'I' of the author; the loss of freedom is more than repaid by the more salient effect of the picture. Precision, individuality is given to it by this pair of eyes, known and named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person limits and specifies the field of vision and supplies personal tone and colour that belong to the story. It helps delimit scope and gives the narrative edge and identifiable stance. Beware: the first-person must mean something in the story (not merely be a mask for the author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of drama — reserve scenic enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the novelist's highest light... to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoard scenic, dramatized scenes for important occasions (climaxes, major turnings) rather than dissipating them on trivial moments. Overuse of scenes in ordinary novels wastes their heightened power; be economical so scenes retain impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and manage transitions between narrative and scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of a novelist appears very clearly in his management of the two, how he guides the story into the scene, how he picks it out of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan how narration will lead into enacted scenes and how to extract the story back into summary or reflection. Good transitions increase richness and coherence; poor ones can make scenes feel extraneous or narration thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unverifiable authorial information (authorial intrusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: He will draw the reader aside and pour into his ear a flow of information... information which will never have its due weight with the reader, because it reposes upon nothing that he can test, for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on aside-commentary or authoritative asides that readers cannot confirm within the story. Such intrusions reduce the picture's authority. Prefer dramatized verification or put the information in a narratively accountable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator an active participant when the subject requires it
rubrics_metrics.description: It would then be like a play within a play; the outer framework at least — consisting of the reflective mind — would be immediately in front of the reader... it would do double duty; it would authenticate and so enhance the picture; it would add a new and independent interest as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the book's subject is the narrator's own growth or consciousness (e.g., Harry Richmond), the narrator must be dramatized and made distinct — not merely a window — so that the story both shows the world and enacts the narrator’s development.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person can unify rambling or autobiographical narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero gives the story an indefeasible unity by the mere act of telling it... the first person will draw a rambling, fragmentary tale together and stamp it after a fashion as a single whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person to bind episodic or digressive material into a coherent whole when the narrator's ownership of events provides unity. But beware of using first-person as a device to excuse formlessness; it is a compositional help, not a panacea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify narrator's position: make the point of view measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: We know who it is that so sees her, and we know where the seer is placed; his line of sight... is measurable, its angle is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate whose eyes the reader uses and where that seer stands in relation to events and characters. A measurable, located point of view gives clarity and objectivity to the pictured scene and makes character-representations weightier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let narration authenticate and add independent interest
rubrics_metrics.description: It would authenticate and so enhance the picture; it would add a new and independent interest as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for narration that both verifies the picture and becomes an engaging element in its own right. The act of telling should contribute to the book's effects, not merely report them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatization to recover intensity lost by pictorial breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom which the pictorial method gives to the novelist is unknown to the playwright; but that freedom has to be paid for by some loss of intensity... the loss is made good and there is nothing to pay at all, so far may the dramatizing process be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When broad, pictorial narration diffuses intensity, counterbalance by introducing dramatized scenes or enactments at key moments so the overall work retains both breadth and emotional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate narrator–story relation; don't leave it a loose end
rubrics_metrics.description: There is felt to be an unsatisfactory want of finish in leaving a question hanging out of the book, like a loose end, without some kind of attempt to pull it back and make it part of an integral design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve or incorporate how the narrator stands to the tale within the novel's design. A persistent unexplained narrator presence weakens the work on rereading; fold narratorial relation into the structure or dramatize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure narrator's voice belongs to the book (not an external commentator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who and what is this 'communicative participator in the business, this vocal author? He does not belong to the book, and his voice has not that compelling tone and tune of its own... which makes a reader enjoy hearing it for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a narratorial voice that feels intrinsic to the fiction—has authority, tone, and reason for being—rather than an external critic's commentary. If the voice is merely the author's aside, it will reduce the picture's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose point of view to serve the book's subject (world-focused vs character-focused)
rubrics_metrics.description: It comes to this, that the picture which Harry Richmond gives of his career has a function essentially dramatic... In Copperfield, Dickens's only care was to represent the wonderful show that filled his hero's memory... the subject is Harry Richmond; the subject is not the cycle of romance through which he happens to have passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel's subject is the panorama of life (favor omniscient or broad retrospective narration) or the individual's emotional/moral development (favor first-person or dramatized focalization). Align POV with whether the book's purpose is to portray a world or to enact a life.
